Why this Comparison page differs
The unit of analysis is database agreement, not centre performance. Recent-paper and researcher/institution leaderboards are therefore omitted; repeating them here would invite comparisons based on unequal source coverage. OpenAIRE is shown as DOI enrichment and a separate exploratory keyword search, not as a symmetric acknowledgment corpus finder.
Two databases, asked the same question independently. Scopus and Web of Science each searched their own funding-acknowledgment text for TRUBA, with no shared method beyond the same term list — so their disagreement here is evidence about coverage, not an artifact of how the corpus was built. (OpenAIRE is compared separately, on the three-database page — its API has no acknowledgment field, so it plays a different role.)

Journal quality

Q1 share of ranked articles, and whether the two databases put the same paper in the same quartile.
measureScopusWeb of Science
Q1 share (ranked)48.0%56.7%
ranked articles2,4042,029
On the 1,623 shared papers: 99% get the same quartile; 7 differ while both are ranked; 9 are ranked in one database and unranked in the other.
Both arms use the same SCImago SJR tables and the same year-matching rule; they differ only in the join key (Scopus source-id first, WoS ISSN alone). WoS also stamps records with a journal's current ISSN, so for 217 WoS articles the ISSN was found only in a neighbouring table year and that year's quartile was used — without that fallback those papers would read unranked purely because their journal changed ISSN.

Citations on the same papers

Both databases count citations from their own index, so these are different quantities measuring the same thing. This DOI-matched view is the fair citation comparison: annual citation bars on the two source pages also use different source-defined corpora, where one highly cited exclusive paper can dominate an apparent yearly gap.

Why is each paper in only one database?

Every exclusive paper looked up in the other available source by DOI rather than by acknowledgment, so "missing" can be split into source-record absence and an acknowledgment-metadata gap. The table above carries the reason per paper.

“Absent from the other database” is decided by DOI lookup, and a Web of Science record may file its DOI under either of two identifier types. Reading only the first hid 55,009 DOIs — 4.7% of the snapshot, concentrated before 2008 — and inflated apparent coverage gaps at the expense of the metadata and wording explanations. Both types are read here.

Web of Science began indexing funding-acknowledgment text in August 2008. Earlier papers carry none at all, so no acknowledgment search can reach them whatever the wording — in this snapshot 0.8% of 2007 records hold any funding text, against 9.9% in 2008 and 28–38% from 2009 onward. Pre-2008 work appears here only where the record was loaded years after publication. Sparse early years are a property of the index, not evidence that little was acknowledged. A Scopus-only verdict on a pre-2008 paper therefore says nothing about whether WoS holds the record.

The 406 WoS-only papers — why Scopus's search missed them

reasonpaperssharekind
in Scopus — no funding data at all33081%metadata

Read the two absence categories differently. 170 Scopus-only papers (22%) have no DOI record in the available WoS project snapshot; this is not proof that the current public WoS Core Collection lacks them. Conversely, 11 WoS-only papers (3%) were absent from Scopus when its live API diagnosis was run. The remaining 620 and 395 papers are present in the available comparison source but arrive without a usable acknowledgment.

A confirmed example is DOI 10.1142/S0218271806008735: it is absent from this project's archived WoS DOI index but visible in the current WoS Core Collection interface. Its WoS acknowledgment-field status remains unknown until the full record or an export containing funding text is inspected.

The two databases fail differently. WoS carries acknowledgment text for only 266,094 of 941,683 records with a DOI (28%) — when it has the text it keeps it in full, but often it has none. Scopus more often records something, but its fund-sponsor is a single value: a paper crediting several funders keeps one and drops the rest, which is how a TRUBA acknowledgment disappears from a paper Scopus otherwise indexes.

So neither database is simply better here, and a single-database acknowledgment study understates its corpus either way.
Method. Scopus and Web of Science were each searched independently for acknowledgment text naming TRUBA, using the same term list. Journal articles only. Records matched across databases by DOI (lowercased). Quartiles from SCImago SJR matched to each paper's publication year. Sources: truba Scopus query + reviewed acknowledgement queue · scan.ndjson .
